sourceBindings.text: Assess, Alert, Attend is a way to organize your response. Assess means quickly checking what has happened and whether you can help safely. Alert means bringing the right help. Attend means giving appropriate assistance within your training. These are connected responsibilities; they are not a rule that you must finish a long checklist before starting urgent care.

Before approaching, look for moving machinery, traffic, fire, damaged electrical equipment or chemical fumes. Keep yourself and other people out of danger. If the area is unsafe, do not enter it to attempt a rescue. Warn others and call trained responders from a safe place. Becoming a second casualty makes the emergency worse.

Identify whether the incident involves an injury, illness or chemical exposure. Look for how many people are involved and what you can actually observe about their condition. Report observations rather than inventing a diagnosis. Conditions can change, so keep checking the scene and the people while help is on the way.

Think of someone falling beside a road. Before rushing over, you would check approaching traffic and whether it is safe to reach them. If they are seriously hurt, you call for help and reassure them. Offering support does not mean pulling an injured person to their feet: pain or an unusual limb position may signal an injury that movement could worsen.

sourceBindings.text: For an ambulance emergency in Egypt, call 123. This number follows the training location, not the language selected in the course. Before fieldwork, the trainer must confirm the site's emergency contacts, access route and backup communication arrangements. If the course is used in another country, confirm that country's emergency number before the activity.

For a serious emergency, summon emergency medical help immediately and alert the supervisor. Do not wait for a supervisor's permission before making an urgent emergency call. Ask another person to call when that allows you to begin necessary assistance safely. Stay on the line and follow the call handler's instructions.

Give five kinds of information: the exact location and an access landmark, GPS position or field number; what happened; the number of people affected; their observed condition; and hazards that are still present. Mention a blocked gate or unsafe approach. Give only facts you know, and say clearly when something is uncertain.

Use a direct instruction such as, 'Please call 123, tell them our field number and come back to confirm the call.' A vague shout of 'Someone get help' may leave everyone assuming another person is doing it. If there is no signal, use the agreed radio or safe backup route without sending another person into danger. Keep a helper with the casualty whenever possible.

sourceBindings.text: First aid is immediate help while professional care is being arranged. It does not make you a doctor or qualify you to perform a procedure you have not learned. Use suitable protective equipment to reduce contact with blood or chemicals. If a person becomes unresponsive or is not breathing normally, tell emergency services immediately and follow their instructions, using only skills you have been trained to perform.

For an accessible bleeding wound, use clean gauze or a clean cloth to apply steady, firm, direct pressure. Arrange urgent help for severe bleeding and keep watching the person's condition. If an object is embedded in the wound or bone is exposed, do not remove it or press directly onto it; protect the area and follow trained emergency guidance. This lesson does not teach wound packing, tourniquet use or other advanced procedures.

A fracture is a break or crack in a bone. A sprain affects the supporting tissues around a joint. A field observer cannot reliably diagnose the difference. Severe pain, an unnatural limb position or inability to move safely requires medical help. Do not straighten, pull or test the injured limb, or make the person walk to prove that it is all right. Keep them still and supported in the position found when the area is safe. Immobilize or move them only within appropriate training and emergency guidance.

Reassure the person and protect them from becoming cold or overheated. In a serious physical-injury situation, do not give food or drink while waiting for medical advice. That instruction must not be confused with small sips of water for an alert person with heat exhaustion who can swallow safely. Never give a drink to someone unconscious, confused or unable to swallow safely.

sourceBindings.text: Prevention starts before symptoms: plan drinking water, rest and shade, and tell the trainer when conditions or your health change. Stop work if you or a partner becomes unwell. Finishing a sample is never more important than responding to illness.

Heat exhaustion can involve heavy sweating, cool or clammy pale skin, headache, nausea, dizziness and weakness. Move the person out of the heat to a cool, shaded place when that can be done safely, loosen unnecessary clothing, cool with wet cloths and fanning, and arrange medical assessment. An alert person who can swallow safely may take small, frequent sips of cool water. Stay with them and keep watching for deterioration.

Heatstroke is a medical emergency. Confusion, unusual behaviour, slurred speech, a seizure or loss of consciousness in someone exposed to heat demands urgent action. Their body may feel very hot and the pulse may be rapid. The skin may look flushed and may be dry or the person may still be sweating heavily. You do not need to wait for sweating to stop or for a temperature reading before calling for help.

Call 123 immediately for suspected heatstroke. Begin rapid cooling while help is coming: get the person to a cooler place if safe, remove unnecessary outer clothing, wet the skin or use cool wet cloths, and fan them. Continue cooling and observation while following the emergency call handler and trained responder. Do not force drinks into a confused or unconscious person. A temporary improvement does not cancel the need for emergency assessment.

sourceBindings.text: The site's chemical plan must identify the product, its safety data sheet, suitable protection and accessible washing equipment before the product is used. A safety data sheet, or SDS, explains the hazards and product-specific response. Section 4 gives first-aid measures. You should not have to search for an eyewash route after a splash has happened.

For the liquid soil-test reagent or fertilizer splash considered here, start flushing the affected eye immediately with plenty of clean, gently flowing water when you can do so safely. Have a helper summon medical help at the same time. The minimum of 15 minutes in this exercise is not an instruction to stop when a timer rings: continue according to the product's first-aid instructions and medical guidance, including while awaiting responders when advised. Do not delay the first rinse while someone retrieves the SDS.

For the liquid reagent-on-hands scenario, immediately begin washing the exposed skin with plenty of clean running water and get help. Avoid contaminating yourself while assisting. The product-specific first-aid instructions govern any further decontamination and removal of contaminated clothing. Dry powders and unusual chemicals can require different handling; do not treat every substance as the same liquid reagent.

Do not rub the eyes or try to neutralize a chemical with another chemical. A small eyewash bottle can start washing, but its presence alone does not prove that the site has enough suitable flushing fluid. The trainer must check the full washing arrangements for the actual hazard before work. If the surrounding atmosphere is hazardous, withdraw to safety and alert trained responders; do not become another exposed casualty.

The site's chemical plan must identify the product, its safety data sheet, suitable protection and accessible washing equipment before the product is used. A safety data sheet, or SDS, explains the hazards and product-specific response. Section four gives first-aid measures. You should not have to search for an eyewash route after a splash has happened.

For the liquid soil-test reagent or fertilizer splash considered here, start flushing the affected eye immediately with plenty of clean, gently flowing water when you can do so safely. Have a helper summon medical help at the same time. The minimum of fifteen minutes in this exercise is not an instruction to stop when a timer rings: continue according to the product's first-aid instructions and medical guidance, including while awaiting responders when advised. Do not delay the first rinse while someone retrieves the SDS.

For the liquid reagent-on-hands scenario, immediately begin washing the exposed skin with plenty of clean running water and get help. Avoid contaminating yourself while assisting. The product-specific first-aid instructions govern any further decontamination and removal of contaminated clothing. Dry powders and unusual chemicals can require different handling; do not treat every substance as the same liquid reagent.

Do not rub the eyes or try to neutralize a chemical with another chemical. A small eyewash bottle can start washing, but its presence alone does not prove that the site has enough suitable flushing fluid. The trainer must check the full washing arrangements for the actual hazard before work. If the surrounding atmosphere is hazardous, withdraw to safety and alert trained responders; do not become another exposed casualty.

sourceBindings.text: Locate the field first-aid kit, including the kit in the work vehicle, and check that people can reach it. Report missing, damaged, used or expired supplies to the trainer. A closed box labelled first aid does not prove its contents are complete or usable.

Know the purpose of the listed equipment: assorted adhesive dressings and sterile gauze pads; adhesive tape and antiseptic wipes; tweezers and scissors; an emergency blanket; written emergency contact numbers; and suitable eyewash provision where chemicals are used. Gauze or a clean dressing helps with direct pressure on a cut. A blanket helps prevent chilling where appropriate. Scissors and tweezers are tools for trained use, not permission to remove embedded objects.

Pain relievers and allergy medicines may appear in a site's documented arrangements. Their presence is not permission for a student to give them to another person. Storage and administration must follow the site's policy and the responsibilities of appropriately trained personnel. Do not improvise a dose or replace emergency care with medication.

Practise three matches: a chemical eye splash needs immediate suitable flushing; a deep cut needs a clean dressing or gauze for direct pressure, with tape available for a trained dressing task; and an emergency call needs written contact and location information. Written contacts remain useful even if you carry a phone: stress, a flat battery or a different person making the call may otherwise cause delay.
